title: Anna Göldi Executed in Glarus: Traditionally Cited as Last European Witch Execution
description:
Anna Göldi, a maidservant in the household of physician Johann Jakob Tschudi in Glarus, Switzerland, was executed on June 13, 1782, following charges that she had bewitched Tschudi's young daughter by causing her to vomit pins and needles. Göldi was not formally charged with witchcraft under that name — by 1782 the Swiss Confederation had no witchcraft statute in force — but was instead charged with 'the employment of poisonous arts' (veneficium). She was tortured, confessed, and was beheaded. The case attracted immediate attention across Europe as a shocking anachronism: Enlightenment commentators, including those writing in the Schleudern gazette, denounced it as a 'judicial murder' and a disgrace to an age of reason.

Historians have debated the precise character of the Göldi case and whether it should be classified as a witch trial at all. The formal charge was poisoning rather than witchcraft, and the motivations behind the prosecution appear to include personal and political factors within Glarus's tight-knit patrician society — Tschudi had reasons unrelated to genuine witchcraft belief to want Göldi removed. Nevertheless, the supernatural elements of the accusation (pins and needles vomited, bewitchment of a child) and the torture-confession dynamic place it firmly in the tradition of witch prosecution even if the formal legal framework differed.

Göldi's case became a cause célèbre in Switzerland and she was formally rehabilitated by the Canton of Glarus in 2008 — over 225 years after her death — through a resolution declaring her the victim of a judicial murder. A museum in Mollis commemorates her case. The Anna Göldi case has been used in subsequent popular and scholarly discussion as a marker of the extreme end of witch prosecution in Europe, though historians note that informal mob violence and social persecution of suspected witches continued well into the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.
historiographical_note: The Göldi case has been the subject of a Swiss popular and scholarly literature including Walter Hauser's research that contributed to her 2008 rehabilitation. Wolfgang Behringer's historical survey of witch persecution discusses Göldi within the framework of the declining phase of European prosecution. The case is treated by Brian Levack and others as a late outlier rather than representative of mainstream prosecution practices, but it retains symbolic significance as a marker of the prosecution era's end.
source_method: Glarus court records; contemporary newspaper accounts; published scholarship on Swiss witchcraft
